subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Socratic Method: Destroying Arguments with Questions
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Socratic Method: Destroying Arguments with Questions.

hook.text: Socrates never told anyone they were wrong. He just asked questions until they realized it themselves.

buildup.text: The Socratic method: a series of targeted questions that expose assumptions, contradictions, and gaps in reasoning.

discovery.text: The pattern: 'What do you mean by X?' 'How do you know that?' 'What if the opposite were true?' 'Can you give an example?'

twist.text: Socrates was executed for it. Powerful people hate being shown they don't know what they're talking about.

climax.text: Modern use: law school, medical training, and therapy all use Socratic questioning to develop deeper reasoning.

punchline.text: The right question is more powerful than the right answer.

quiz.question: What is the Socratic method?
options: A series of questions that expose assumptions and contradictions in reasoning

details.summary: The Socratic method uses carefully sequenced questions to expose contradictions in someone's beliefs. Instead of asserting your view, you guide the other person to discover flaws in their own reasoning.
details.whyItMatters: Questions lower defenses and invite self-reflection in ways that direct confrontation cannot, making the Socratic method powerful for teaching and persuasion.
takeaways: Questions can be more powerful than assertions
The method teaches people to think rather than what to think

faq.question: What types of questions are most effective in the Socratic method?
faq.answer: Clarification questions ('What do you mean by X?'), probing assumptions ('Why do you believe that?'), and consequence questions ('What follows from that?') work best. Each peels back a layer of unexamined belief.

faq.question: Why is the Socratic method more effective than lecturing?
faq.answer: People resist being told they are wrong but accept conclusions they reach themselves. The Socratic method makes the listener the active discoverer of truth rather than a passive recipient.
